synth.hackGoal: Sundai Hack 143 asks one question: how can we measure how fast someone is aging using data we can collect today, from things like a face photo, a phone camera, a wearable, voice or a simple movement test [F51, F52]. In 12 hours, teams build an AI app from scratch and put it on a public URL. At 20:00 an audience of researchers, hackers, clinicians and longevity enthusiasts votes on what they saw. The bar a credible entry has to clear: the result should rest on published evidence that the measure tracks aging, not only on a model that guesses a person's age in years [F42, F46].

winFactors.factor: Voters can try it on themselves in the room
winFactors.why: The vote happens straight after the 20:00 presentations. A demo that each voter runs on their own phone in under a minute is remembered and voted for. A slide is not.

winFactors.factor: Scientific honesty that a researcher and clinician audience will respect
winFactors.why: The Biomarkers of Aging Consortium says the field lacks standards and consensus on what makes a reliable aging biomarker [F46]. The validation template it points to is test-retest reliability plus association with morbidity and mortality [F42]. A team that shows its sources, its error and its limits will beat one that overclaims, because this crowd knows the literature, and the Consortium's conference starts the next day [F52, F53].

winFactors.factor: Linked to aging outcomes, not only to guessing age in years
winFactors.why: Many off-the-shelf models predict chronological age only. One example is the open voice age model, with an error of 7.1 to 10.8 years [F33, F34]. Entries backed by a measure that is associated with mortality or morbidity after adjusting for age will look more like a biomarker.

winFactors.factor: A working app on a public URL by 20:00
winFactors.why: Sundai's format is to build a new AI app from scratch by the end of the day [F51]. If it is broken or offline on stage, it is out of the running.

winFactors.factor: Visible AI that is not a copy of an existing app or of what the crowd is building
winFactors.why: FaceAge is the headline example in the organizers' brief, and its code is public [F14], so several teams are likely to build selfie age. Phone apps for camera sit-to-stand [F55] and fingertip-pulse body age [F56] already exist, so an entry needs a clear angle and should credit the prior art openly.

ideas.name: Movement Age
ideas.oneLiner: A browser app that uses on-device pose estimation from a phone or laptop camera to time a one-leg stand and count sit-to-stand repetitions, then places each result on a published age-band reference table, with the source shown.
ideas.rationale: This is I21's two-test design, framed around an age-band result. Reference studies exist for both tests across adult ages: unipedal stance in 549 healthy adults aged 18 and over, in six age bands from 18 to 39 up to 80 and over [F22], and 5-rep, 30-second and 1-minute sit-to-stand percentiles by sex and age in 393 Colombian adults [F23]. The per-band numbers are not in the abstracts and still have to be read from the full texts. Failing a 10-second one-leg stand was associated with all-cause mortality after adjusting for age, sex, BMI and comorbidities (HR 1.84, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.78), but only in adults aged 51 to 75 (unverified) [F21]. Remote video sit-to-stand assessment showed good to moderate validity against in-person testing [F24], though that used human raters, not pose estimation. No pose-specific validation study was found. Live demo scores 4, not 5, because the camera has to see the whole body, so the phone must be propped up or held by a friend. The result must be shown as an age band, not an exact year, because the youngest band in F22 covers 18 to 39.

ideas.name: Chair-Rise Age (merged with I51)
ideas.oneLiner: The phone browser camera counts sit-to-stand repetitions with in-browser pose estimation and returns a percentile against a cited age and sex reference table.
ideas.rationale: I21 and I51 are the same idea. They are kept under ref I21 and scored here as the single sit-to-stand variant from I51, because I21's two-test version is scored above as PRIOR. Sit-to-stand reference values exist [F23], but the files have no mortality evidence for sit-to-stand alone. The only outcome link is a composite fitness age (chair stand plus grip, walking speed and peak flow) in adults aged 60 and over, which was associated with depressive symptoms and cognitive impairment [F26]. A phone sit-to-stand app already exists on iOS [F55], so on its own this has the weakest differentiation of the movement options. It is the easiest to build.

ideas.name: Count vs Tap
ideas.oneLiner: A validity check: the camera counts chair stands while a person taps a button for each rep, and the app shows live agreement between the two.
ideas.rationale: On its own this is a measurement check, not an aging measure, so science is low. It speaks directly to the reliability part of the validation template [F42], and remote sit-to-stand assessment has published validity and minimal detectable change values (6.6 and 10.5 reps) from a post-COVID cohort [F24]. It is best used as a feature inside PRIOR, not as a product of its own.

ideas.name: AgeGap Selfie Lab
ideas.oneLiner: A browser app that takes a face photo and a back-of-hand photo and shows a photo-age estimate next to the user's stated age, with an uncertainty band and a consent and bias panel.
ideas.rationale: A selfie is the fastest live demo. The science behind FaceAge is about cancer patients: they looked 4.79 years older than a non-cancerous reference cohort [F11], and older FaceAge was associated with worse survival [F13]. The FaceAge repo says it is not for clinical or commercial use [F14], and no current permanent weights link was confirmed (L1 gap), so a substitute model would not carry that evidence. The only hand-photo evidence in the files did not survive review, no hand-age model weights were found, and hand images carry identification risk [F16]. FaceAge is the organizers' first suggested direction, so many teams are likely to build this.

ideas.name: Age-Gap Evidence Board
ideas.oneLiner: An interactive explainer where users place a photo-age gap against cited published effect sizes and see what an age gap does and does not mean.
ideas.rationale: It is honest and low-risk, and it cites real findings [F11, F13, F42]. But it measures nothing new, and the AI is minimal. That is a poor fit for Sundai's build-an-AI-app format [F51]. Its best parts would work as a credibility panel inside another app.

ideas.name: Regularity Check
ideas.oneLiner: Load an Apple Health export or a sleep CSV and get a sleep regularity score computed in the browser.
ideas.rationale: The mortality evidence is unverified, and review restricted it: the UK Biobank cohort averages 62.8 years and used 7 days of wrist accelerometer data, so the mortality figures must not be applied to adults aged 20 to 70 (unverified) [F31]. The finding that regularity predicts mortality better than duration carries the same restriction (unverified) [F32]. The formula for the score and the quintile cutoffs were not retrieved (L3 gap). Voters would have to export health data on stage, which does not fit in 60 seconds.

ideas.name: Three-Signal Aging Panel
ideas.oneLiner: In 60 seconds, the webcam and mic capture face-video heart rate, a heart-rate-variability proxy and a voice age estimate, shown as a labelled panel with error bars.
ideas.rationale: The most vivid AI on stage, but the weakest science. The open voice model predicts chronological age with an error of 7.1 to 10.8 years [F33, F34]. Contact-free face pulse was less accurate than fingertip pulse, especially after exercise [F35]. The files hold no evidence that resting heart rate from a camera tracks aging. Running a large voice model in the browser and keeping face pulse stable in hall lighting are both real risks in 7 hours.

ideas.name: Clock Report Card
ideas.oneLiner: Load any aging-clock output as a CSV and get a one-page validation report card in the browser: error against chronological age, test-retest reliability and association with risk factors.
ideas.rationale: It mirrors the DunedinPACE validation template of reliability plus outcome association [F42], and it addresses the lack of standards the Consortium names [F46]. Voters cannot try it on themselves. The public cohort data and clock coefficients it needs are not established in the files.

ideas.name: Pace Not Age
ideas.oneLiner: A pace-of-aging composite from two time windows of wearable data that reports a rate of change with confidence intervals and split-half reliability.
ideas.rationale: It borrows the idea of aging as a rate rather than a level from DunedinPACE [F41], but the files hold no evidence that a wearable composite tracks aging. It needs a personal data export, so a room demo is impractical.

ideas.name: Aging Clock Arcade
ideas.oneLiner: A web app that combines a face photo, a 30-second sit-to-stand and a finger-camera pulse into one multi-signal age with uncertainty bars for each signal.
ideas.rationale: It matches the organizers' suggestion to combine modalities, but no published method in the files combines these signals into one age, and the per-signal reference ranges it assumes are not in hand. Fingertip camera pulse is accurate for heart rate in healthy young adults [F35], but a phone-camera body-age product using fingertip pulse already exists [F56]. Three captures will not fit in 60 seconds.

ideas.name: Look Age vs Move Age
ideas.oneLiner: Side-by-side results for one person: a face-photo age estimate next to the Movement Age balance and chair-stand bands, so you see whether you look your age and whether you move it.
ideas.rationale: A combination of PRIOR and I11. The movement half carries the evidence [F21 (unverified), F22, F23]. The face half would need a licensed in-browser model. FaceAge is research-only [F14], and its weights link is unconfirmed (L1 gap), so the face half adds AI spectacle but not much evidence. Best treated as a stretch goal on top of PRIOR.

ideas.name: Pulse plus Pose
ideas.oneLiner: Movement Age plus a fingertip-camera heart rate before and after the chair stands, shown as separate domain bars rather than one fused number.
ideas.rationale: Fingertip camera heart rate is accurate at rest in healthy young adults [F35]. The files hold no evidence that heart rate from a phone camera tracks aging, and a deep-learning pulse age exists only as a preprint, with no weights established [F36]. A fingertip-pulse body-age app already exists [F56]. Showing domains separately rather than as one number follows the per-organ argument in proteomic aging [F45], but that is an analogy, not evidence for these signals.

pick.name: Movement Age
pick.oneLiner: Prop up your phone, do a one-leg stand and five chair stands, and on-device pose estimation places each result on a published age-band reference table, with the source shown and nothing leaving the device.
howItWorks: Open the public GitHub Pages URL on a phone or laptop. A start screen says that nothing leaves the device and that this is not a medical device and does not diagnose anything. The user picks their sex and age band, because the reference studies report results by sex and age band [F22, F23].

Prop the camera so the whole body is in frame. In-browser pose estimation (for example MediaPipe Pose loaded from cdn.jsdelivr.net) draws a live skeleton, and a framing check waits until hips, knees and ankles are visible.

Balance test: the timer starts when one ankle lifts and stops when that foot comes down. It takes the best of three tries, matching the reference protocol [F22], and marks the 10-second point, the threshold studied in adults aged 51 to 75 (unverified) [F21].

Chair test: reps are counted when the hip and knee angles cross standing and sitting thresholds, and the app reports the 5-rep time or the 30-second count, both of which have reference values [F23]. A teammate or friend can tap a button on each rep, and the app shows camera count against tap count (from I22).

Lookup: each result is compared with the age-band tables transcribed from the full texts of F22 and F23. The app reports which band's typical performance it matches. For example: your balance matches the band typical of ages 40 to 49. It never gives a single year, because the youngest F22 band spans 18 to 39.

Result card: balance and leg strength are shown as two separate bars, each naming its source study, cohort and limits. It ends with the line: an estimate from published reference data, not a medical device, not a diagnosis.

whyChosen.reason: It is the only idea where every voter can test themselves in the room and the result rests on published reference values that span adult ages, for both tests.

It is the only phone-friendly test in the files with a mortality association after adjusting for age, sex, BMI and comorbidities. It is narrow (adults aged 51 to 75) and unverified, so it is shown as context, never as a prediction about the user.

Remote video assessment of sit-to-stand already showed good to moderate validity against in-person testing. Adding a live tap check turns that into a visible measured error, which fits the reliability-first validation template this audience uses.
It fits the build: static site, pose estimation runs on the device, no server, no training. Tables and threshold logic are about 7 hours of work for two people with Claude Code.
It stays out of the crowd most likely to build selfie age, and out of FaceAge's research-only terms and unconfirmed weights. The hand-age evidence did not survive review.

killCriteria.statement: A published reference table for the chosen tests covers adults from roughly 20 to 80.
killCriteria.note: Pass on coverage, but the numbers are NOT in hand. Unipedal stance norms cover 549 healthy adults aged 18 and over, in six bands from 18 to 39 up to 80 and over [F22]. Sit-to-stand percentiles by sex and age cover 393 Colombian adults, reported as aged 18 to 80, though review saw a mean age of 44 and could not confirm the range in the fetched text [F23]. Neither abstract gives per-band values, so both full texts must be read and transcribed before results can be shown. The 18 to 39 band means no age-in-years result is possible for younger users, so the pitch line 'you move like a 31-year-old' must become an age band.

killCriteria.statement: Evidence that the measure predicts mortality or morbidity beyond chronological age.
killCriteria.note: Narrow pass. Inability to complete a 10-second one-leg stand was associated with all-cause mortality in a model adjusted for age, sex, BMI and comorbidities, HR 1.84 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.78), in 1702 adults aged 51 to 75 [F21]. The file marks this unverified (the script quote check failed), although three reviewers upheld it from the Europe PMC abstract. It must not be extended to people under 51. For chair stands, the only outcome link is a composite fitness age (with grip, walking speed and peak flow) associated with depressive symptoms and cognitive impairment in adults aged 60 and over, in a cross-sectional design [F26]. Nothing in the files covers ages 20 to 50.

killCriteria.statement: The 10:30 intro does not hand out data, a model or a prize that favours another modality.
killCriteria.note: Wilson judges this live at 10:30. No co-host or named speaker is listed for the intro [F51], so its content is unknown. If it releases a face or wearable dataset, or a prize for a specific modality, re-score before pitching at 11:00.

killCriteria.statement: No teammate brings a better idea at 11:00.
killCriteria.note: Wilson judges this at team formation. Any competing idea should be scored on the same five criteria, with live demo and science weighted most.

pick.differentiation: A camera sit-to-stand app already exists. F55 is an iOS app that scores the chair-rise test from 240 frames-per-second video and reports time, velocity and muscle power [F55]. Its 'scientifically validated' label is the developer's own claim, not independent evidence, and it is Apple-only. Movement Age should name it openly as prior art in the README and on stage, and should not compete with it on biomechanics. What differs: Movement Age runs in any phone or laptop browser with no install, combines a balance test with the chair test, and its output is a placement on published age-band reference tables, with the source study and cohort shown for each number. The F55 finding does not describe an age-referenced readout. It also differs from the existing phone body-age app, which uses fingertip pulse plus a questionnaire [F56]. Movement Age shows its sources and its measured counting error, rather than a single body-age score.
risks: The reference values are not in hand. The F22 and F23 abstracts give no per-band numbers, so if the full texts cannot be opened by about 13:00 there is nothing honest to compare against. Fallback: report raw time and reps with the study bands described, and no placement.
No study validating pose estimation for rep counting or balance timing was found (L2 gap). The tap check is the only accuracy evidence the app will have, so it must work.
Framing: the full body has to be in view. Voters using their own phones in a crowded room need a friend to hold the phone, or a propped-up laptop. Test in the venue's lighting and space before 20:00.

Reference transfer: F23 is a Colombian sample tested under supervision, F22 dates from 2007, and chair height and arm position protocols were not retrieved (L2 gap). Ordinary chairs vary, so a mismatch in chair height may shift results.
Scope creep in the mortality claim. F21 covers ages 51 to 75 only and is unverified. Showing it to a 25-year-old as if it applied to them would be wrong.
Safety: a one-leg stand can cause a fall. The app should tell users to stand next to a wall or chair back.
Other teams may also build movement, since it is a suggested direction. The tap check and the sources-shown card are the differentiators to protect.
stretch: Test-retest card: each test is done twice, and the difference is shown against the minimal detectable change from the remote sit-to-stand study, labelled as a post-COVID cohort [F24].
Eyes-closed stance variant, which the unipedal norms also cover [F22].
Fitness-age equation from the Korean adult model [F25], only if the coefficients can be read from the full text, labelled as based on supervised fitness-centre data.
A result card image generated in the browser for sharing, with no server.
Look Age vs Move Age (NEW-1), adding a face estimate beside the movement bands, but only with a model whose licence allows it.

synth.pitch30s: Hi, I'm Wilson. Today's question is how fast someone is aging, using data we can collect now. I want to build Movement Age. Open a web page, prop up your phone, and on-device pose tracking times a one-leg stand and counts your chair stands. We place you on published age reference tables for both tests [F22, F23], with the source shown. It is not a medical test, and nothing leaves your phone. I need someone strong in front-end or computer vision. Who's in?
demo60s: 0 to 10 s: a QR code on screen. 'Open this on your phone now. No install, nothing leaves your device.'
10 to 25 s: a volunteer does a one-leg stand on stage. The live skeleton shows, the timer runs, the 10-second mark lights up, and the result appears as an age band with its source study shown [F22].
25 to 40 s: five chair stands. The camera count and a teammate's tap count appear side by side, with the agreement figure, so the room sees the measured error [F24].
40 to 50 s: the room tries it. Voters do a one-leg stand at their seats, holding a chair back, and see their own result card.

50 to 60 s: a credibility card listing what each number rests on (F22, F23, and F21 marked unverified and limited to ages 51 to 75), F55 credited as prior art, and the line 'an estimate from published reference data, not a medical device'. Then the open-source repo link and the ask for votes.
synth.teammateAsk: First, a front-end or computer-vision builder comfortable with JavaScript and in-browser pose estimation. They own rep counting, stance detection and the framing check, which together are the main technical risk. Second, if a third person joins, someone who can read research papers (a researcher, physical therapist or clinician). They would get the F22 and F23 full texts, transcribe the age-band tables accurately before about 13:00, and help defend the science to the clinicians who vote.
openQuestions: Can the full texts of the Springer 2007 unipedal stance norms [F22] and the Colombian sit-to-stand reference values [F23] be opened today, and are their age bands fine enough to report a useful band for each user?
What does the app show users under 40, given that the youngest F22 band spans 18 to 39?
Can F21 be verified from the full BJSM text? It is unverified in the file because the script quote check failed.
Does in-browser pose estimation count reps and detect foot-down reliably on ordinary phone cameras in the i-lab's lighting, and at what distance?
What chair height and arm position do the F23 tests use? This was not retrieved, and it changes how comparable a voter's result is.
Will the 10:30 intro release data, a model or a prize that favours another modality (K3)?
Sundai's actual judging and voting rules, team-size rule and open-source requirement were not confirmed from sundai.club (L5 gap). Wilson's notes are the only source.
How many other teams pick movement or sit-to-stand? That decides how much the tap check and sources card need to carry the differentiation.

appliesWarnings.F31: Claim omits the population and protocol. The cohort averages 62.8 years and sleep regularity came from 7 days of wrist accelerometer data, which a single unsupervised camera session cannot reproduce. Do not use the mortality figures for ages 20 to 70. The 20-48 percent range was not verified; I saw HR 0.52 and 0.70.
